opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a really interesting comparison, because on the surface both look like hard dynamic control problems, and in some sense they are. But I think the key difference comes down to contact.

With a quadrotor, you're dealing with a system that's essentially in free space. The dynamics are complex, but they're well understood — you have thrust from four rotors, gravity, some aerodynamic effects — and you can model that quite precisely. Once researchers worked out good controllers and had fast enough sensors and processors, the stability problem became, I wouldn't say trivial, but tractable. That's why you can now buy a drone for a couple hundred dollars that hovers beautifully.

Walking over rough terrain is a different beast, because the robot is constantly making and breaking contact with the world. Every time a foot hits the ground, you have this discontinuity — friction, slipping, the ground deforming, a rock rolling underneath. Those contact events are notoriously hard to model and simulate. Small errors in where the ground is or how it responds get amplified. And the robot can't see the terrain perfectly, so there's uncertainty in perception on top of uncertainty in physics.

What's been remarkable in the last several years is that legged locomotion has improved dramatically, largely through reinforcement learning in simulation with lots of domain randomization — you train the policy over thousands of variations of terrain, friction, masses, so it becomes robust to what it doesn't know. That's why we now see quadrupeds walking up hills and over rubble quite well.

But I'd emphasize that locomotion is still easier than manipulation. When you walk, you're mostly contacting a relatively static ground with your feet. When you grasp and manipulate objects, the contacts are more intricate, the objects move, and the variety is enormous. So I think of it as a spectrum: flight is the most tractable, legged locomotion has gotten much better, and dexterous manipulation is still the frontier — that's where we really have a long way to go.

r001.rationale: The response says walking requires continually making and breaking contact with the world, unlike a quadrotor operating in free space, and describes contact uncertainty as a source of difficulty.

r002.rationale: The response mentions training across terrain variations to improve robustness, but does not say that tolerance for terrain differences makes the effective legged-locomotion state space lower-dimensional.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a great question, and I think the answer is a little counterintuitive to people, because when you watch a quadrotor hovering perfectly still in the air, that looks like magic, and when you watch a robot dog stumbling over some rocks, that looks like it should be the easy one. We've had dogs doing this for millions of years. But the physics are actually very different.

With a quadrotor, you're dealing with a system that's nonlinear, sure, and it's unstable in the sense that if you turn the motors off it falls out of the sky. But it's remarkably well-behaved. You have four rotors, you can model the thrust each one produces, you can model the aerodynamics reasonably well, and crucially, the environment it's interacting with is air. Air is smooth. It's continuous. If you push a little harder, you get a little more lift, and the relationship is predictable. So you can write down a model, you can linearize it around hover, you can put a controller on it, and it works. Once people figured that out in the mid-2000s, it got very good very quickly, and that's why you can buy a drone for a few hundred dollars that will hold its position in a breeze.

Walking is a completely different animal, literally. The hard part isn't the robot, it's the ground. Every time a foot comes down, you're making contact, and contact is where the mathematics gets ugly. You have friction, which is notoriously hard to model. You have impacts, which are discontinuous: one millisecond the foot is in the air, the next it's bearing load. You don't know exactly when that transition will happen because you don't know exactly where the ground is. Is it going to be solid rock? Is it going to be gravel that shifts under you? Is it mud? Is the rock going to roll? And the robot has to decide where to put the next foot before it knows the answer. So you have this hybrid system that's switching between different dynamic regimes, and the switching is governed by things you can't observe very well.

And then there's the fact that a quadrotor's environment is essentially the same everywhere. Air over a parking lot is like air over a field. Rough terrain, by definition, is never the same twice. So you can't just tune a controller for one case.

What's interesting is that the recent progress on legged robots has come largely from giving up on modeling all of that precisely and instead using learning, training in simulation with lots of randomized terrain so the controller gets robust to the uncertainty rather than trying to eliminate it. That's a very different philosophy from the quadrotor story, which was really a triumph of classical control. I think it tells you something about where the difficulty lies: when you can model the world well, you control it; when you can't, you have to learn to be forgiving of your own mistakes.

r001.rationale: It says each foot must make contact with the ground and explains that friction, impacts, and uncertain contact make walking difficult, unlike flight through air.

r002.rationale: The response says rough terrain varies and controllers must handle uncertainty, but does not explain that tolerance for terrain differences makes the effective state space lower-dimensional.

astra-6.text:
There’s a slightly counterintuitive distinction here: flying can actually be easier than walking. A quadrotor is moving through air, and although there are disturbances, you have a relatively consistent set of dynamics. You can measure its orientation and continuously adjust the thrust to keep it stable.

With a quadruped on rough terrain, every footfall introduces a new interaction with the world. Where exactly is the surface? Is it solid? Will the foot slip? As a foot makes or breaks contact, the forces acting on the robot change abruptly. And you have to coordinate those contacts while keeping the body balanced.

So it’s not simply a question of how many motors you’re controlling. A lot of the difficulty comes from contact and uncertainty. Flight is certainly challenging, but walking over terrain you don’t know requires you to repeatedly establish—and rely on—physical contacts whose properties you may not know very well.

r001.rationale: It says rough-terrain walking requires repeatedly establishing physical contacts with uncertain surfaces and forces, making it harder than quadrotor flight.

r002.rationale: It does not identify reduced effective state-space dimensionality or explain it through robots’ tolerance for different terrain configurations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the surprising thing is that flying can be easier than walking. That sounds backwards, because we tend to think of flight as this extraordinary capability. But a quadrotor, once it’s in the air, has fairly continuous dynamics. You can measure its orientation and make rapid adjustments to the thrust of its motors to keep it stable.

A quadruped on rough terrain has to deal with contact. Where do you put each foot? When it touches down, is the ground where you expected it to be? Is it firm, or does it give way? Is the foot going to slip? Every time a foot lands or lifts off, the forces acting on the robot change. And those decisions are coupled: where you put one foot affects where you can put the next one.

So neither problem is trivial, but walking brings together perception, planning, and control in a particularly challenging way. Animals make it look effortless, which can obscure just how much is going on.

r001.rationale: It explains that quadrupeds must manage foot placement and changing contact forces on rough terrain, making walking especially challenging compared with flight.

r002.rationale: It discusses terrain variation and foot placement, but does not say that robots’ tolerance for terrain differences reduces the effective dimensionality of the locomotion state space.
